groups.title: Urban beekeeping
groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: A lecturer talks about urban beekeeping.

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about something that might surprise you: keeping bees in cities. Many people assume that bees need open countryside, but in recent years urban beekeeping has become surprisingly popular, and it's attracting scientific attention too.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: The modern movement began around two thousand and eight, when a group of enthusiasts in New York started placing hives on rooftops. Before that, keeping bees in the city was actually illegal there, so those first beekeepers had to campaign for a change in the law.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Since then the idea has spread widely. In London alone there are now about seven thousand hives, which is far more than twenty years ago. Paris, Berlin and Tokyo have also seen rapid growth, often supported by local councils and companies.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Now, you might wonder whether bees have enough space to find food in a crowded city. In fact, a worker bee can travel up to five kilometres from the hive, although most of them stay much closer. That is a large area, even in a big city.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: I should explain why this matters. Bees are responsible for pollinating a large share of the fruit and vegetables we eat, so anything that helps their numbers is good news for food production as well as for the environment.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Within that range, a city offers a great variety of flowers. Gardens and parks are the main sources of food, and many streets also have trees that produce a lot of nectar. Because people plant flowers for decoration, there is something in bloom for most of the year.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Interestingly, bees in the countryside often have more difficulties. Large farms grow just one crop, so there are long periods with no flowers at all, and farmers also use pesticides, which can harm the bees and reduce their numbers.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: That's why some city hives actually produce more honey than rural ones. But keeping hives on a roof isn't without challenges. The bees need a regular supply of water, especially in hot weather, so beekeepers usually put a shallow container beside the hives.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: The honey itself has a distinctive character. Beekeepers in many cities report that honey from the summer months has a strong, sweet taste, because the bees visit the lime trees along the streets. Honey from other seasons can be quite different.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Of course, there are risks. The most serious problem for bees worldwide is a small insect called the varroa mite, which spreads disease between hives and can destroy a whole colony within a single season.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: This is a serious issue, because the disease can travel from one hive to another on bees that wander into the wrong entrance. Neighbouring beekeepers therefore need to communicate with each other regularly and share information.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: To control this, beekeepers should inspect each hive regularly, usually every ten days in summer, although some people check weekly when the weather is warm. Early action is the key to protecting the colony.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Finally, if you're thinking of trying this yourself, please don't just buy a hive and hope for the best. Most councils recommend that new beekeepers attend a training course, which usually lasts a whole weekend and includes practical work with real bees.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: Some people worry about safety, but honeybees are gentle, and rooftop hives are placed away from busy areas. Neighbours rarely notice them unless the beekeeper tells them.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE

transcript.text: To sum up, urban beekeeping shows that cities can be good places for wildlife if we plan them carefully. Thank you for listening, and I'm happy to take questions now.
transcript.speaker: DR ROSE
